Production Operations

1. Production Operations

A production system creates obligations. Someone must know when it is failing, who may change it, how to recover it, and what evidence supports its service promises. HarborWorks now moves from “the site works” to an operating model that other people can rely on.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch031.xhtml — Chapter 29 — Production Operations

2. Make a change reviewable and reversible

Record the pre-change state, expected result, rollback trigger and post-change service verification. A green process-status indicator substitutes for the user-facing acceptance check.

SOURCE: Make a change reviewable and reversible

3. Chapter 29 — Production Operations

A production system creates obligations. Someone must know when it is failing, who may change it, how to recover it, and what evidence supports its service promises. HarborWorks now moves from “the site works” to an operating model that other people can rely on.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch031.xhtml — Chapter 29 — Production Operations

4. 29.1 Development vs. Production

Development favors rapid exploration; production must also protect users, data, and continuity. The difference is not that production never changes. It is that changes have defined owners, tests, exposure limits, and recovery paths.

Keep representative test environments without copying sensitive production data casually. Differences in kernel, security policy, certificates, identity, or network topology can make a development success misleading.

A single production-like VM is useful for functional validation, but cannot reproduce every fleet, concurrency, or failure-domain property. State which tests it supports and which require a larger environment.

Linux example — 29.1

Record which host and identity a procedure would affect.

What to check: Environment classification also requires an authoritative inventory and service owner.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch031.xhtml — 29.1 Development vs. Production

6. 29.2 Change Management

A change record describes the purpose, affected systems, prerequisites, implementation, validation, rollback, owner, and decision authority. The rigor should match the consequence: editing a harmless label differs from changing root storage or authentication.

Record both planned and emergency changes. During an incident, approval can be accelerated under policy, but the action still needs a scope and evidence trail. Reconcile the successful repair into configuration management afterward.

Do not let a checklist become a substitute for understanding. “Backup complete” should point to a usable recovery point and tested procedure, not merely an unchecked assumption copied from yesterday’s ticket.

Linux example — 29.2

Save a change worksheet in a new local workspace.

What to check: Concrete test and rollback steps make a proposed change reviewable.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch031.xhtml — 29.2 Change Management

8. 29.3 Maintenance Windows

A maintenance window coordinates permitted disruption, staffing, dependencies, and communication. Define what work may occur, when to stop, and how long rollback needs. Starting a risky step near the end of the window without rollback time defeats the purpose.

Notify affected teams with the actual expected impact. “Server restart” is an implementation detail; users need to know whether requests fail, sessions end, or background jobs pause.

Some changes can be performed without visible interruption using tested redundancy and draining. That is an engineered property, not something guaranteed by calling a change “rolling.” Verify remaining capacity and dependency behavior before removing a node.

Linux example — 29.3

Record time and active sessions before planned work.

What to check: Match the maintenance window's timezone and service dependencies; these commands do not authorize downtime.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch031.xhtml — 29.3 Maintenance Windows

10. 29.4 Patch Management

Patch management inventories assets, evaluates applicable advisories, tests updates, stages deployment, verifies running state, and tracks exceptions. A package downloaded to a cache is not installed; an installed kernel is not necessarily running.

Define patch urgency from exposure, vendor guidance, service risk, and available mitigations. Record unsupported systems and owners rather than allowing them to disappear from reports because the normal tool cannot update them.

Reboots, service restarts, and compatibility checks belong in the plan. Rollback may require configuration and data compatibility, not only an older package. Automate routine checks while keeping explicit stop conditions for failed health tests.

Linux example — 29.4

Inspect updates without applying them.

What to check: Stage and validate the intended transaction before scheduling installation and reboot.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch031.xhtml — 29.4 Patch Management

12. 29.5 Configuration Drift

Drift is divergence between declared and observed configuration. It can result from manual changes, partial rollouts, package defaults, compromised processes, or another automation system. Not every difference should be erased without inspection.

Classify the difference: approved emergency repair awaiting reconciliation, unauthorized change, generated runtime state, or an error in the declared baseline. Reconcile the correct intent and retain evidence.

A drift detector must understand ownership. Comparing every byte under /var with an image snapshot produces noise because much of /var is expected to change. Monitor the properties that should remain controlled.

Linux example — 29.5

Detect drift in a controlled local file.

What to check: The check should pass; store authoritative production baselines in a protected managed system.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch031.xhtml — 29.5 Configuration Drift

14. 29.6 Monitoring

Monitoring collects signals about systems and services. Combine internal measurements with external checks of user-visible behavior. Internal metrics help explain failures; external probes can detect paths the host cannot see.

For HarborStatus, measure a correctly named HTTPS request with certificate verification and an expected content marker. Also observe process restarts, filesystem capacity, memory pressure, and backup age. These measurements answer different questions.

Monitor the monitoring path. A missing probe result can be a failed collector rather than a healthy service. Treat stale data and gaps explicitly. Google’s SRE guidance distinguishes service symptoms from internal causes and emphasizes selecting actionable signals. (R63)

Linux example — 29.6

Observe service state and an independent endpoint.

What to check: Manager state and request success are different checks; use the intended hostname for actual acceptance.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch031.xhtml — 29.6 Monitoring

16. 29.7 Metrics

A metric is a defined numeric observation over time. Counters accumulate events, gauges describe a current quantity, and histograms summarize distributions under chosen buckets or another representation. Know how the collection system interprets each.

A service-level indicator, or SLI, measures an aspect of service behavior. A service-level objective, or SLO, sets a target for that indicator over a window. An agreement with consequences is a separate contractual matter. (R63)

For a teaching SLI, define successful requests as valid requests returning the correct marker within a selected latency limit, divided by all valid requests in the window. Document exclusions and low-traffic behavior. A number that silently removes every failed request is not measuring availability honestly.

Linux example — 29.7

Sample resource metrics.

What to check: Preserve units, timestamps, and workload context for trends.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch031.xhtml — 29.7 Metrics

18. 29.8 Logs

Logs provide event context that aggregate metrics often omit. Use consistent timestamps, service identities, severity, and request correlation where possible. Protect private data and avoid logging credentials or unnecessary payloads.

Central collection should preserve enough origin information to distinguish hosts and instances after replacement. Retention, access, transport protection, and ingestion failures need owners.

Do not confuse a log line declaring “backup complete” with verified recovery. Logs report what code observed or chose to report. Correlate them with stored artifacts and tests appropriate to the claim.

Linux example — 29.8

Read a bounded service log window.

What to check: Retention and centralized delivery need separate validation.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch031.xhtml — 29.8 Logs

20. 29.9 Alerting

An alert should identify an actionable condition, a responsible responder, and a useful first step. Immediate paging is appropriate for conditions requiring immediate intervention, not every transient threshold crossing.

Use duration, severity, suppression, and grouping deliberately. Alerting separately on every failed probe during one network outage can overwhelm the responder. Conversely, suppressing all alerts during a long maintenance window can hide unrelated failures.

Test delivery and escalation. An alert rule that evaluates correctly but sends to an abandoned address does not provide coverage. Include the service, impact, observation time, and runbook location without embedding secrets.

Linux example — 29.9

Create a simple threshold check for your lab shell.

What to check: A useful alert also needs routing, deduplication, ownership, and workload-specific thresholds.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch031.xhtml — 29.9 Alerting

22. 29.10 Availability

Availability describes whether a service is usable under a defined measurement. It can be measured by successful requests or by time-based checks, but those definitions are not identical. State the window and what counts as success.

For illustration, a 99.9 percent time-based target over exactly thirty days allows 0.1 percent of 43,200 minutes, or 43.2 minutes, outside the target. That arithmetic does not define a real agreement, prove an architecture can achieve it, or settle whether maintenance counts.

Correctness matters. Returning HTTP 200 with the wrong data is not success for a service whose purpose is accurate status. Choose indicators that reflect the actual user contract.

Linux example — 29.10

Bound an availability request.

What to check: Replace with the intended service and add content verification; one successful request is not an availability history.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch031.xhtml — 29.10 Availability

24. 29.11 High Availability

High availability uses architecture and operations to limit service interruption under specified failures. It requires independent enough components, failure detection, failover, data handling, and sufficient remaining capacity.

Two web processes on one host protect against some process failures but not host loss. Two VMs on one physical host share that host’s failure domain. Two application servers sharing one unprotected database still depend on that database.

Write the failure assumptions before buying or configuring more nodes. Then test them. Redundancy that exists only in a diagram is not established failover behavior.

Linux example — 29.11

Resolve the service name before checking failover design.

What to check: Multiple addresses alone do not prove redundant failure domains or working failover.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch031.xhtml — 29.11 High Availability

26. 29.12 Load Balancing

A load balancer distributes work and can remove unhealthy backends according to its configured checks. It must itself have an availability design appropriate to the service. One unprotected proxy in front of two servers can become the central failure point.

Define connection draining and readiness during deployments. Stop admitting new work before shutting down a backend, allow existing work to finish under bounded rules, and verify reintroduction after the change.

Applications must handle shared or external state appropriately. A user session stored only in one backend’s memory can fail when traffic moves, even though every server passes a generic health check.

Linux example — 29.12

Inspect an HTTP endpoint's headers.

What to check: Headers do not prove which backend was used; correlate with approved backend identifiers and load-balancer logs.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch031.xhtml — 29.12 Load Balancing

28. 29.13 Redundancy

Redundancy provides alternate components, but correlated failure can defeat apparently separate copies. Shared power, storage, network paths, credentials, configuration errors, and administrators can connect their outcomes.

A uniform bad configuration rolled out to every node is a common-mode failure. Staging and canaries introduce an operational separation even when the hardware is already redundant.

Evaluate how maintenance affects reserve capacity. A design with one spare may lose its failure tolerance while that spare is unavailable for an update. Document the resulting risk window rather than claiming unchanged resilience.

Linux example — 29.13

Inspect local RAID and mounted resources.

What to check: Hardware or provider redundancy can be outside this view; redundancy still does not replace backup.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch031.xhtml — 29.13 Redundancy

30. 29.14 Scaling

Vertical scaling increases resources within a node; horizontal scaling adds nodes. Vertical scaling can be simpler but may require interruption and has platform limits. Horizontal scaling can improve capacity and failure isolation while adding distribution and state-management complexity.

Measure the bottleneck first. Adding web nodes does not necessarily help a saturated shared database. More concurrency can even increase contention.

For HarborStatus’s static content, replication is comparatively simple because immutable release files can be deployed identically. A write-heavy transactional service needs a different consistency and recovery design. Do not generalize the static-site exercise into a universal scaling recipe.

Linux example — 29.14

Observe capacity before proposing scale changes.

What to check: Scale the bottleneck demonstrated by workload evidence, not simply the resource easiest to buy.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch031.xhtml — 29.14 Scaling

32. 29.15 Runbooks

A runbook describes how an operator handles a specific situation. It should include symptoms, prerequisites, read-only checks, decision points, approved changes, rollback, verification, and escalation. Commands need explicit targets and assumptions.

A runbook is not a transcript to paste wholesale. Include stop conditions such as “the device identity does not match” or “the second administrative login fails.” Explain what evidence leads to the next step.

Store the runbook where it remains available during the incident it describes. Periodically ask another operator to execute it in a lab. Missing assumptions become defects to repair before a real outage.

Linux example — 29.15

Create an executable read-only runbook step.

What to check: A complete runbook also names prerequisites, stop conditions, and escalation owners.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch031.xhtml — 29.15 Runbooks

34. 29.16 Incident Management

Incident management coordinates restoration, investigation, and communication. Assign an incident lead, technical operators, and communication ownership according to scale. Keep one current state record so responders do not unknowingly make conflicting changes.

Prioritize user impact and data integrity. It may be appropriate to disable a harmful feature or roll back a release before completing diagnosis. Record why the decision was made and what evidence was preserved.

Use explicit handoffs: current symptoms, confirmed facts, actions taken, remaining hypotheses, risks, and next checks. An exhausted responder’s undocumented mental model is not a sustainable operating system.

Linux example — 29.16

Record an incident timestamp and a bounded snapshot.

What to check: Keep an evidence timeline and assign responsibility before experimenting with repairs.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch031.xhtml — 29.16 Incident Management

36. 29.17 Postmortems

A postmortem records impact, timeline, causes and contributing conditions, detection, response, and corrective actions. A blameless approach examines why actions made sense given available information while still assigning ownership for improvements.

Avoid hindsight certainty and vague fixes such as “be more careful.” Prefer changes that can be verified: add a named-host test, constrain a deployment target, automate a rollback check, or remove a shared credential dependency.

Track action completion and effectiveness. Publishing a thoughtful report without implementing its controls leaves the same operational risk in place. Distinguish confirmed causes from remaining uncertainty. (R63)

Linux example — 29.17

Write a postmortem outline.

What to check: Tie actions to demonstrated failure mechanisms and measurable follow-up.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch031.xhtml — 29.17 Postmortems

38. Requirement

Release a new HarborStatus marker to two independently recoverable lab servers while preserving a known-good copy. The exercise assumes both are already configured and an operator can direct test traffic to either server. It does not claim a production load balancer exists.

Define the acceptance test before deployment: correct hostname, trusted TLS, expected marker, no new service errors, and latency within the agreed lab envelope. Save the prior content and configuration revision.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch031.xhtml — Requirement

39. Staged execution

Update web1 only. Test it directly while preserving the intended name with curl --resolve. Compare its release marker and logs with web2. If any required test fails, stop expansion and restore web1 from the prior revision. Do not update web2 in the hope that consistency will make both healthy.

After a defined observation period and explicit acceptance, update web2 and repeat the same checks. In a real load-balanced deployment, draining, readiness, and capacity checks are additional steps around each host change.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch031.xhtml — Staged execution

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch031.xhtml — Staged execution

41. A useful failure

Suppose the new page returns HTTP 200 but omits the expected marker. The release is rejected because transport success does not meet the content contract. Record the missing acceptance behavior and keep the healthy version available while correcting the artifact.

The value of the canary is not that it never fails. It is that a failure is observed before the change reaches every copy.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch031.xhtml — A useful failure

42. Practice and implementation lab

Write a one-page runbook for “HTTPS responds with the wrong release.” Include a named-host request, a certificate check, content verification, configuration inspection, rollback, and escalation. Have another learner identify the stop conditions without asking the author.

Check your understanding. Does redundancy eliminate common-mode failure? No. Is a metric useful without a definition and time window? Not reliably. Does a completed postmortem mean its corrective actions are complete? No.

Chapter takeaway. Production reliability comes from measured service contracts, controlled change, and rehearsed response—not from the absence of visible alarms.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch031.xhtml — Practice and implementation lab

43. Apply a rollback trigger from an acceptance contract

A release-record model exercises an explicit rollback decision; it does not deploy a real service. The solution checks the stated outcome explicitly. These fixture results do not establish that a real privileged service is configured correctly.

SOURCE: Apply a rollback trigger from an acceptance contract
